Chicago, Dec. 1.—In the presence of hundreds of patrons of the Great Northern theater Special Policeman Milan E. MESSENGER' BOYS RIOT.
They Fight the Negro Men Who Have Displaced Them in Atlanta.
Displaced Them in Atlanta.

ATLANTA, Ga., June 27.—Two hundred white messenger boys were thrown out of employment at a o'clock this afternoon by the Western Union and Postal Telegraph companies and their places filled with negro men. The action of the two companies is taken after a full consideration of the situation. The officials of both companies say that it is done to get better service.

As a result of the change, rows have been the order around the headquarters of the telegraph companies to-night. It was feared to use negro boys, as it was well known that the white boys would not be long in running them off the streets. The grown men employed by the telegraph companies have fared little better, as the boys have banded together and a mob of them has attacked the messengers every time they leave the office.

Six boys jumped on one negro at Western Union headquarters and bruised him badly before the office force could rescue the negro. The management then had to call on the police to clear the office of boys, but they are hanging around and miss no chance to attack their successors. As both companies have made the change the boys will hardly have a chance to institute a boycott, but they say that they will continue to make it lively for the negro messengers and force the companies to take them back.

FIGHT NEGRO MESSENGERS.
Discharged Telegraph Boys in Atlanta Have a Riotous Sunday.
ATLANTA, Ga., June 28.—The white messenger boys discharged by the Western Union and Postal Telegraph companies yesterday afternoon have had a day of revenge and the negro men hired in their places have been dodging stones since the first messages began to go out this morning.

Banded together, the boys have been lurking around the streets in gangs of eight and ten, and the luckless negro who has come into their sight carrying a telegram has been a quick victim, unless a patrolman could reach the scene to protect him from assault.

Several negroes were bruised badly by such assaults. Several times the police have had to scatter the boys gathered around the telegraph headquarters, but they leave the offices to go out to meet the negroes in guerrilla warfare.

The 200 boys were discharged because they would not wear the uniform and because the company thinks the negroes will give better service.
atlanta-atlanta-1903-06-28.A3:
HARD TIME FOR NEGRO MESSENGERS.
Discharged Whites in Atlanta Keep Them Busy Dodging Rocks.
Atlanta, Ga., June 28.—The negro messengers substituted for white boys by the Western Union and Postal Telegraph companies have had a hard time to-day and to-night dodging rocks thrown by the discharged boys, and the police have been kept busy all day trying to protect the negroes.

The companies hired grown men to take the places of the boys, but this has not kept the boys from getting their revenge. They have gone about in bands, and when a negro wearing the badge came into sight he has been immediately attacked.

Several negroes have been badly hurt by rocks and others have been bruised in personal encounters. Several times the police have had to scatter the boys from the telegraph headquarters, but the latter have kept up their desultory warfare and say that they will never allow the negro messengers to hold their places.

May, a constable of Buffalo township, Pike county, has attracted fovorable notice by his cool nerve in preventing the lynching of two young negroes who were charged with attempted assault on a white woman. A large crowd gathered to hang the culprits, but May hustled them away right under the eyes of the would-be lynchers before they had time to organize. SHOULD HAVE LYNCHED HIM
Negro Fiend in Reno Assaults a White Woman in a Lodging House
The Reno Journal says: Charles Peters, a negro commonly called "Harry," is occupying a cell in the county jail this morning and is glad he is there. If he hadn't been taken from the city prison to the more inviunerable structure he might be hanging to the Virginia street bridge today.

Peters took a drink or two yesterday and the brute in him came to the surface. He went into the lodging house kept by John Dotta, over the Reno Wholesale Liquor Store, and looked through the rooms. In one of them he found Mrs. Dotta, who was making up the bed.

The negro said: "I want to ee you privately." He entered, closed the door and locked it. Mrs. Dotta ordered him from the place, but the negro approached her and seized her.

Mrs. Dotta's screams caused one of the lodgers to run to the Opera House saloon, kept by Mrs. Dotta's husband. The latter hurried over to Commercial street in search of a policeman. He found Officer Tatum, but by the time they reached the lodging house the negro had taken fright and escaped.

Officer Tatum arrested Peters at the south entrance of the Virginia street subway and took him to the city jail.

Mrs. Dotta was in a pitiable condition. Her clothes were in tatters as the result of her fight with the black fiend. She was hysterical and for a time her codition was serious. This was made all the worse by the fact that she is soon to become a mother.

The circumstances became noised about and the officers feared that an attempt might be made to lynch the negro and he was conveyed to the county jail by Officers Berry and Tatum for safe-keeping.

At midnight Mrs. Dotta had nearly recovered from her fright and exertions. It is learned that the prisoner is a rounder who fequents the tenderloin and is accused by the officers of living off the earnings of a woman of his own color.

A later report, in today's Journal, says:

Last night was one of vague alarms. There were rumors current that an attempt would be made to lynch the negro who assaulted Mrs. Dotta with intent to commit rape. The victim was somewhat better yesterday but had not fully recovered from the physical and nervous shock. The clothes were torn from her as she resisted the attempts of the brute.

All night there were gatherings upon the street corners and in sequestered places where there was whispered conversation relating to the heinous offense. It seemed at one time as though an attempt would certainly be made to advance on the jail, and lynch the prisoner, but wiser counsel prevailed.

WHITE CAPS SCARE NEGROES.
Labor in Barbour County, Alabama, Is Badly Demoralized.
Montgomery, Ala., August 21.—(Special.)
A well authenticated rumor reaches here from Barbour that there is a practical race war on in one portion of the county and as a result negroes are being driven out of the county by whitecaps.

A prominent citizen of Barbour was in the city yesterday to see Judge Jones, of the United States district court, and ascertain what methods could be adopted to stop whitecapping, which was seriously demoralizing the labor of the county.

It is understood that Judge Jones referred the Barbour county citizen to the governor, saying: "I do not think the federal authorities should be called on to do what the state authorities ought to do, and have it in their power to do."

The Barbour citizen went to the capitol to see the governor, but the governor being absent at Blount Springs the private secretary, J. Kirk Jackson, promised to lay all the facts before the governor immediately on the governor's return to the capitol.

It is said that the labor on three or more large plantations in Barbour have been run off by whitecaps and labor generally in that section of the county where whitecapping is said to have occurred is greatly demoralized.

The cause for this outbreak against negroes in Barbour is not known here. But it is said to be due to some overt acts of the negroes, who have made themselves obooxious to certain people of the neighborhood.

ping" Negroes.

Federal Court to Prosecute
Men From Barbour.
Five of Them Arraigned and Advised
by Judge Jones to Secure Lawyers—Statements of the Crime.
Six indictments against white citizens of Barbour County charging "white capping" were returned yesterday by the United States grand jury for the Middle District of Alabama, with a list of twenty-two indictments returned in a partial report to Judge Thomas G. Jones.

The indictments are against Jesse Green, Bufort McCall, Morgan Padgett, John Green, James Sanders and Richard Knowles, all citizens of Zeiglers postoffice, Beat 8, Barbour County. They are charged with violating Section 5508 of the Revised statutes of the United States, relative to conspiracy by two or more persons to injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate any citizen in the free exercise or enjoyment of any constitutional privilege.

Persecuted Negroes.

The indictments charge the men with having violated this section in the cases of Albert Barefield, Marion Shipman, Hillard Turner and Nancy Miles, negroes.

Jesse Green, Bufort McCall, Morgan Padgett, John Green and James Sanders were yesterday afternoon arraigned in open court.

At that time, it was indicated that all five men would plead guilty and ask for the mercy of the court.

There is not a bad face among the five men. All the men are rough and illiterate in appearance. Three of them are splendid specimens of physical manhood. They seemed to be awed by the solemnity of the court.

Judge Jones, presiding, stated to the prisoners the seriousness of the charge against them. He said that he understood that they considered themselves, not liable to federal prosecution on account of having been tried in the State courts for an assault and battery on one of the negroes, whom they are alleged to have "whitecapped."

Judge Jones informed the prisoners that the prosecution in the State courts for assault and battery could give them no good plea of former jeopardy. He told the men that if they wanted to, and knew they were really guilty, they could enter pleas of guilty. On the other hand if they desired a trial, he wanted to impress upon them that a fair and unbiased hearing would be given them.

One man said he would like to make a statement in reference to his position.

Judge Jones told him that if he intended to plead not guilty it would be best for him to make his statement to a lawyer.

"Just Naturally" Innocent.

"Well, Judge, I jés naturally ain't guilty," declared the prisoner. The others nodded approval.

"In that case," said the Judge, "I would advise you to engage a good lawyer and when you engage him, make a clean breast of the affair to him. He will know what is best for you to do."

The men signified their intent to follow the court's advice. Their cases were set down for a hearing Thursday and they were released on bonds.

Julius Sternfeld, Assistant District Attorney, in open court, when repeating the government's proof to the court, made remarkable statements.

Lash Laid On a Man Until He Is So Weak He Cannot Stand.
Fayette, Mo., Feb. 9.—A race war has been started here as the result of the public whipping of three negroes on the Courthouse steps on Friday night. A committee of the Law and Order League took three negroes from their homes and whipped them publicly for alleged misconduct. Two of them were women. DRIVING OUT THE NEGROES. Race Troubles at Fayette-Whitecaps Establish a Whipping Post.
St. Louis, Feb. 9.—Reports brought here to-day indicate that a race war is on at Fayette, Mo. Owing to the lawlessness of the blacks and their insolent bearing toward white women, a law and order league has been formed by the better class of citizens, several clergymen among the number, and at a recent meeting it was resolved to establish a whipping post for drunken, immoral and otherwise generally objectionable personages.

As a result three negroes, a man and two women, were forcibly dragged from their homes at night by men disguised as white caps and publicly whipped. The man made a vigorous fight before he was overpowered, and cursed and threatened the white caps even as the lash was cutting his bared back. He was so beaten that he had to be cared for by physicians. The women were taken to the outskirts of the town and ordered to depart and never return.

A white man who has been fraternizing with the negroes has barricaded himself in his house and refuses to leave. He threatens to shoot any one who attempts to molest him. Many blacks are leaving the town.

Former Senator Clark, who brought the news to this city, says bloodshed is almost certain to follow, as both sides are determined and armed.

Both Sides Waiting for Developments in Race Trouble at Fayette, Mo. MORE WHIPPINGS IMMINENT. Unless Other Disreputable Negroes Leave the City the Vigilance Committee Will Take a Hand.
BY A STAFF CORRESPONDENT.

Fayette, Mo., Feb. 10.—After the social disturbance here Saturday night a peace, rather foreboding in its intensity, has settled over the town and both sides are rather anxiously awaiting further developments.

As the result of a law and order meeting held at the Courthouse on the night of February 2, a vigilance committee was formed that meted summary judgment upon certain disreputable characters and warned them to leave town at once. Three women and one man were publicly whipped in a severe manner. When released two of the women at one left town, but the other woman has so far refused to obey the commands of the vigilance committee.

The man, Bill Smith, was too severely injured to make his escape the night of his punishment. He was found early the next morning wandering about town in a semiconscious condition and was taken in charge by some people of his own race, who gave him medical attention. This morning he was arrested upon an old warrant charging hog-stealing and he is now in the County Jail. He will be tried upon that charge as soon as his physical condition permits.

KILLING CAUSE OF THE RACE TROUBLE.

The present agitation against the disreputable negro element had its origin in the killing of Harry O'Donnell, a white man, in a negro resort. O'Donnell was a native of Montpellier, Ind., and was here visiting his brother, who is employed in sinking a shaft for an artesian well near the Katy tracks.

It is alleged that O'Donnell was enticed into the house and killeld. O. L. Turner, Fannie Simpson and Leonard Lyle, negroes, were arrested immediately after the killing and at the Coroner's inquest Lyle and the Simpson woman gave direct testimony against Turner. The latter is a well-known character here and it is said he has been in trouble frequently.

The authorities told me that Turner had cost the county more than $1,700 in prosecutions in the last twelve months, and that he has long been regarded as a disturbing element among the worst class of negroes.

CITIZENS HOLD INDIGNATION MEETING.

The killing occurred on the night of January 27, and popular feeling against the objectionable negro element culminated, less than a week later, in a monster mass meeting, participated in by all classes of citizens. The Reverend Fielding Marvin, pastor of the Methodist Church, was selected chairman. Addresses were made by several of the local ministers.

The feeling of indignation against rowdy negroes became general and the meeting became demonstrative. R. C. Clark, one of the best-known man of the town, focused the sentiment of the people in a stirring speech. He advocated strenuous methods, at the same time stating that the plan for a legal whipping post as advocated by many was entirely out of the question, as that mode of punishment was against the State law.

Warning resolutions were adopted and committees appointed to see that they were enforced. The report of the action taken by the citizens spread rapidly and created great excitement among the negroes affected by the resolutions. The suggestions of corporal punishment for the offenders against public decency also caused comment.

NO WHITE MAN
COULD WHIP HIM.

The negro Bill Smith is said to have

stated in public that no white man could whip him and to have expressed a special animosity against the Town Constable who, he declared, ought to be "plugged." This open defiance of the spirit of the resolutions incensed the public order party and arrangements were quietly made to give the disreputable negroes a lesson that would be long remembered.

A committee was formed, the personnel of which has been conveniently forgotten by everybody here, and Smith was dragged from a saloon, which he was known to frequent. He was taken to a large elm tree near the graveyard and soundly whipped with buggy whips and leather tugs. His back and sides were severely cut.

At the end of the punishment inflicted upon Smith the committee concluded to finish the work by giving a partial warning to several of the more notorious negroes of the town. The women were taken from their beds and hurried in their night clothes to the north side of the Courthouse, where they were thoroughly whipped and warned to leave town immediately.

The day following the action of the Vigilance Committee at least twenty-five negroes left town. Unless several others go in the near future it is said that another lesson will be administered. The members of the committee made no attempt to disguise themselves, but so thoroughly has the spirit of purification taken hold of the citizens that no names are ever mentioned when the matter is referred to. Respectable negroes are not in danger; in fact, many of the better class indorse the extreme measures adopted, and advocate a repetition of the lesson, if necessary. H. G. NICHOLAS.

Grouped around the front door this bright, sunshiny winter day, are, by actual count, twenty-one idle negroes, mostly youths. It was a spectacle to see, reecktly, before our City Council, a large committee of negroes, representing the respectable element among them, asking the city authorities to rid this town of the low class of negroes, harlots, drunkards, loafers and thieves. We find our laws helpless; to imprison them means comfortable winter quarters for them. What would you do?"

That question is both pertinent and perplexing. Of course it will be justly contended that the citizens had no right to whip and drive out these worse than worthless negroes but—What would you do? The editor of The Independent answers the question in a way by saying:

"What would we do is not easy to tell. We would not seize these lawbreakers and whip them and rob them of their property by driving them from their homes, and inflict them on some other community. We would convict harlots, drunkards and thieves and make convict life unpleasant to them with hard work. We would shut up that saloon, which is retained by the will of the white citizens."

That is no answer at all. The class of negroes spoken of cannot be convicted unless they have committed some crime. Nor could the editor "shut up that saloon" without valid cause. There is no charge that any disorderly conduct is allowed in the saloon, or that its not conducted decently. The proprietor has presumably taken out and paid for a license, and if he is guilty of no wrong to shut up his saloon would be treating him with as little respect for law and justice as the negroes were treated whose cause The Independent espouses.

The conditions of which this Marshall County man writes prevail throughout the South. Such sights as he depicts can be seen in Montgomery every bright day in the year. There are idle, dissolute negroes to be seen at every place where one can comfortably loaf. They are men and boys, and sometimes women and girls can be seen. Some of them, at least, are of the classes mentioned by the writer. We cannot convict them because they are idle or because they may possibly be criminal. We cannot whip them and drive them out as our Northern brethren not infrequently do. The fact that they may be harlots and thieves and that they spend all their time in idleness is no valid reason for taking the law into our own hands, or for dealing with them without law, but these conditions do furnish a reason why we listen with little tolerance to the advice of those who know nothing of the conditions. And we are brought back to the question What would you do?

The mob's victims were George McKinney, Garfield McCoy and Wiley Anette, negroes who on last Saturday night cowardly murdered F. S. Bullard, a respectable Baker county farmer.

Bullard had gone to the house occupied by one of the tenants on his place in order to quiet a free-for-all fight that had started among a company of negroes who were engaged in a Saturday night frolic. Six negroes present were more or less seriously wounded during the shooting, and one may die.

McKinney, McCoy and Anette were captured Monday and placed in jail at Newton. Their guilt was fully established at a commitment trial on Tuesday. There was some talk of a lynching, but little attention was paid to it, there being an apparent willingness to allow the law to take its course.

THE BAKER COUNTY LYNCHING.

In our dispatch yesterday in which an account is given of the lynching of three negroes in Baker county early on Friday morning it is stated that the crime is greatly deplored by most of the people of that county. Assuming that this statement is correct, it follows that only a small minority of the citizens approve the lynching.

It is gratifying to know that this is the case. It hasn't been so very long since there were very few lynchings of negroes in the South except for assaults upon white women. Now lynchings for the killing of white men are getting to be quite common. The question which presents itself in this connection is, to what limit will the mob go in lynching alleged law-breakers unless checked? It is evident that unless the strong arm of the law interposes the mob will undertake to administer what it considers justice to many other offenders than those accused of assaulting women.

There does not seem to be any doubt that the negroes who were lynched in Baker county were guilty of killing Mr. Bullard, a farmer who undertook to put a stop to a disturbance among negroes on his place. And the fact that he left a helpless family no doubt aroused a great deal of feeling against the negroes who killed him, but the law ought to have been permitted to take its course. If a mob can with impunity take the law into its own hands whenever it feels like doing so, it will not be long before, in many parts of the state, there will be established a tyranny of such an intolerable character that peace-loving and law-abiding citizens will seek homes elsewhere.

The danger in these lynchings for all sorts of crimes is that the number of lynchings will steadily increase, and will claim victims guilty of no offense, but who have in some way obtained the ill-will of persons wicked enough to arouse the mob spirit against them.

We have not been advised as to the course the authorities of Baker county intend to pursue in regard to the tragedy that occurred there on last Friday morning, but it is quite certain that if something isn't done to make the mob understand that mob violence will not be tolerated, there will be more lynchings in the county, and some of them may not be confined to negroes.

A writer in the New York Evening Post makes the point that the steady increase in the number of lynchings, both in the North and the South, means that the people are demanding a change in the statutory law to meet existing conditions. There has, he says, been an insidious and abnormal increase in crime, and that if lynchings are to cease something must be done to stamp it out.

There may be something in this view, but what is it that it is proposed shall be done? As a general thing the leaders of the lynchers are not those citizens who lead public sentiment. The laws against crimes which are the cause of lynchings are now as severe as they can be made, and in most parts of the country are enforced with a reasonable degree of promptness. It may be that in some cases there is a failure of justice because of delays in bringing offenders to trial, but it is doubtful if such delays are at the bottom of the lynchings. The writer of the article in the Post does not point out what readjustment of the statutory law is needed. The fact that most of the lynchings are brutal and barbarous in character seem to indicate a desire for vengeance rather than a purpose to have punishment, such as the law prescribes, meted out to the wrongdoers.

NEGRO SPIRITED AWAY.
Jail Demolished by a Mob That Was Cheated of Contemplated Prey.
BLUEFIELD, W. Va., March 28.—Harvey Williams, a negro miner, had a narrow escape from summary death last night. Yesterday on a lonely strip of road that leads across the mountains from Pocahontas to Coopers he criminally assaulted the thirteen-year-old daughter of a Mr. Jones, who lives near Bramwell. The little girl, with great effort, managed to reach her home, where she gave the alarm. A searching party soon captured her assailant and placed him in jail. When dark came hundreds of people had assembled in the little town of Bramwell bent on lynching the brute, but officers in citizens clothes led the negro through the crowd and soon had him well on the road to Princeton, the county seat, ten miles distant.

About 11 o'clock to-day the crowd, thinking the negro was still in the Bramwell jail, made an onslaught on the structure with the result that it was practically torn to pieces. Upon finding that the object of their wrath had been spirited away the people's anger was unbounded and hundreds of pistol shots were fired into the air and the mob otherwise showed their disgust at having been foiled.

While Judge Nero Pitchford was a Magistrate, many years ago, he was plowing about a half mile from home when one of his children came out and announced that a neighbor was at the house wanting to see him on important business. The weeds were about to outgrow the corn, but he climbed a large hill and was about worn out when he reached the house. The neighbor's wants were made known after much urging, two hours after the Judge arrived. After hearing the trouble elaborately explained, the Judge gave him some advice and started to return to his work.

The neighbor said: "Hold on. How much do I owe you?"

The Judge told him he did not make any charge, as the law would not allow it.

"Well," said the gentleman, after studying a few moments, "here's a nickel. I guess that will about pay you for your trouble."

MURDERED BY A NEGRO
PROMINENT YOUNG PLANTER KILLED IN TUNICA COUNTY.
ARMED MEN AFTER THE FUGITIVE
Herbert Clifton Is Shot to Death Without Provocation by a Negro, Who Then Made His Escape-Description of the Murderer People in Pursuit.
Robinsonville, Miss., Nov. 29.—Bodies of armed and infuriated men from nearly every hamlet in Tunica and DeSoto counties are scouring the country tonight in search of George Jenkins, a fiendish negro, who ruthlessly shot to death Herbert Clifton, a prominent young planter, at Banks, a station on the Yazoo & Mississippi Valley railroad thirty miles south of Memphis and four miles west of this town, shortly after 6 o'clock this evening. The murderer, if caught, undoubtedly will be summarily put to death. Tonight a posse of forty men, heavily armed and with bloodhounds, left Tunica, the county seat, for the hill lands of DeSoto county, in which direction Jenkins made his flight from Banks. A large crowd of armed men left Robinsonville tonight, and from other villages to which the news of the awful murder has reached men have joined in the mad pursuit of the murderer.

Unprovoked Murder.

The killing of Clifton occurred near the depot at Banks shortly after the accommodation passed, which was about 6 o'clock, and was one of the worst murders ever committed in Tunica county. Clifton is sub-agent of a large plantation near Banks and the negro Jenkins was employed as one of the laborers. The two met near the depot about 6 o'clock this evening, Clifton stopping the negro to talk over a land matter. Suddenly, and without the slightest provocation, Jenkins began to use the vilest profanity, and when Clifton told him to desist he stepped back a few feet, drew a revolver and fired twice at Clifton, both balls taking effect, the first entering the leg and the second burying itself deep in the breast. Clifton was unarmed, and so suddenly did Jenkins bring his deadly weapon into play the former hardly had time to realize that he was facing death. Clifton walked to a store near the depot and fell to the floor, dying thirty minutes later. Jenkins fled immediately after the shooting, going in the direction of the hills cf DeSoto county, which joins Tunica county, near Banks Station.

Description of Negro.

George Jenkins, the murderer, is described as being about 35 or 37 years of age, tall, black and bears a conspicuous scar on the back of his head. He has lived in this section a long time, and his reputation is very bad. He has always been considered a desperate man, with a predilection for using deadly weapons. It is thought he will be caught, for every foot of territory of the surrounding country will be searched by the pursuing posses.

Herbert Clifton, the murdered man, lived at Arkabutla, Tate county, and was temporarily residing in Tunica county, where he had accepted a responsible position on the Banks plantation. His father is John Clifton, postmaster at Senatobia. Clifton married several years ago, and leaves a wife and one child. He was of a kind nature, not the least disposed to be quarrelsome, and stood high both in this native and adopted homes. He never had and previous trouble with the negro Jenkins, and at the time of the tragedy was unarmed.

If Jenkins is not caught tonight more men will join the chase and bloodhounds from other points will be brought here and put on the trail. The officers of adjoining counties have been notified and furnished with a good description of the murderer, whose capture is believed to be only a short time off. That Jenkins will be lynched there is no doubt.

Bruce Cursed Policeman and One Struck Him With His Billy, Whereupon Bruce Fired---- Robertson's Body Taken to Henderson by 1:20 Train.
Policeman J. W. Robertson, who was shot by the negro, James Bruce, in Henderson on Thursday night, died at Rex Hospital last night at half past nine o'clock.

The body was taken to Henderson this morning on the 1:20 train by Rev. J. S. Williams, pastor of the Methodist Protestant church there, and Policeman Oscar Falkner, who came to Raleigh yesterday by the evening train.

The dead man's wife, his son, Roy Robertson, and his daughter, Miss Pearlie Robertson, who came in yesterday morning, also returned with the body.

Bruce's condition was extremely critical up to the time of going to press, but Dr. Hubert Royster stated last night that he would probably live until today.

Immediately upon the arrival of the special train yesterday morning at about half past three o'clock, both the wounded men were taken to Rex Hospital, where Dr. Hubert Royster, assisted by Drs. J. H. Tucker and Hartwell Bass, of Henderson, operated upon them without delay. Both men were placed in the same operating room and the surgeons went from one to the other, back and forth as rapidly as possible.

Policeman Robertson had one bullet wound only, but that was a terrible one. The ball, of 32-calibre, entered just below the curve of the ribs on the right side of the abdomen. Its course was downward, and it pierced the small intestines near the spinal column, making one large rent in the bowels. The hemorrhage was very great, and the wound is so far back that it was difficult to get at it. Then the officer was very stout, and there was a layer of full four inches of fat over the abdomen. His heart, too, was weak, and that made matters worse still. He sank steadily all the time since arriving here.

Bruce has three bullet wounds and a cut over the left eve, made billy of one of the policemen.

One of the bullet wounds is below the cut, but this does not seem to be serious at all.

The other two are in the abdomen. One entered over the stomach and injured the diaphragm, but did not penetrate the stomach at all. The other wound is in the left side, midway between the ribs and the hip. The ball perforated the intestines in four places, taking an upward direction. The four openings were sewed up and the blood washed out of the abdomen.

He took his seat among the white people, and the policeman detailed to the show ordered him to go over to the section set apart for colored people. He objected, but claiming that he had paid for his seat and had a right to it, but behaved quietly and left his seat.

After the show was over Bruce went up to where Policeman J. W. Robertson and Robert Crockett were standing and began cursing them. One of the policemen struck Bruce on the side of the head with his billy, whereupon Bruce began firing, and the policemen returned the fire.

The same gentleman stated that all Henderson is very much stirred up over the affair, and that there is a great deal of feeling over the horrible affair. However, there has been no indication of trouble.

TERRIBLE TRAGEDY.
Two Men Shot to Death and Another Wounded.
Another Wounded.

Henderson Deeply Stirred Over the Awful Occurrence—Policeman John W. Robertson Fatally Shot by James Bruce, Colored, Who in Turn Receives His Death Wound—Policeman R. A. Crockett Narrowly Escapes a Like Fate—His Clothing Punctured by Bullets One Shot Taking Effect in the Breast Inflicting a Slight Wound—The Trouble Brought on by the Negro and Without Provocation.

Henderson has been stirred as never before perhaps by an awful tragedy enacted within her borders last Thursday night. As the result of a trivial matter and extreme fool-hardiness on the part of a young negro two men are dead, a third one narrowly escaped the same fate, two families are plunged into mourning and the community has been full of excitement and false and unfortunate rumors.

Sparks' Show was here Thursday. At the night performance James Bruce, colored, took a reserved seat among the white people. Bruce was a very bright mulatto and could easily be mistaken for a white person by any one who did not know him. He bought a reserved seat ticket the man who sold the tickets (inside the tent near the entrance) taking him to be a white person at the time. Soon after Bruce had taken his seat among the white people Policeman R. A. Crockett's attention was called to his presence. Ponceman John W. Robertson being nearer to Bruce than he was Officer Crockett directed him to tell Bruce that he was in the wrong section and ask him to move. Officer Robertson touched him on the shoulder to attract his attention and so notified him. Bruce hesitated and did not seem disposed to move. When spoken to again he said he had paid for his seat and he had a right to it, the man sold it to him. At this juncture Officer Crockett said "Bruce, you know you are a negro and you ought to have gone on the other side with the colored folks," telling him at the same time to get up and go on without having any trouble. "I am not going anywhere until I get my money (10 cents) back," was Bruce's reply, and Officer Crockett told him he would get it for him. Going to the lady who took up the tickets he stated the case to her and she in turn spoke to the man who sold the tickets. He refunded the money and Officer Crockett gave it to Bruce, who immediately got up and left. This was done so quietly that it attracted no attention, only a few persons who occupied seats close by knowing anything about it. There was no disturbance, no forcible ejection, no excitement whatever and the occurrence was soon forgotten by all save Bruce.

Instead of going on the opposite side and taking a seat among his own people where he belonged Bruce left the show and came down town. He went into Daniel & Co's. hardware store where he was employed (he carried the key) and got his pistol. Arming himself he went back to the show grounds and waited for Officers Crockett and Robertson to come out. When the performance was over and the crowd dispersed they stayed behind looking for some one for whom they had a warrant thinking he might be hanging around the show grounds.

As the two officers came out of the show tent Bruce accosted them. Addressing Officer Crockett he said he wanted an explanation from him about making him move his seat. The officer replied that he had no explanation to make, he was only doing his duty as an officer, and that he (Bruce) knew he was a negro and knew he had no business where he was. At this Bruce began to curse and showed a disposition to bring on trouble. Crockett told Robertson to take charge of the man that he did not want to have any fuss with him. Bruce defied them to put their hands on him saying he had not done anything to be arrested for and he would swim through h—l before he would be arrested, at the same time moving up closer to Crockett in an insolent and threatening attitude. Up to this time no movement had been made to take hold of Bruce and no violence had been resorted to. "You don't know the difference between a d—n nigger and a negro," said Bruce. "There is no difference as far as I know," replied Crockett, whereupon Bruce cursed him and applied a vile epithet which is unfit to print even in the form of abbreviation and dashes.

As he did so Bruce made a motion to draw his pistol. Crockett struck him with his billy but he was not close enough and the force of the lick was not sufficient to knock his assailant down or prevent him from using his pistol. Bringing his weapon into play almost instantaneously Bruce put the muzzle against Crockett's right breast and fired. The bullet, a 32-calibre, produced only a slight flesh wound and was found afterward in his sock having dropped down the leg of his trousers. One shot passed through the front part of his coat, another cut the end of the right coat sleeve and powder burned the cuff, while still another passed through the bottom of the vest—four shots in all leaving their imprint on his person or clothing.

Officer Robertson was standing close by and a little to the right of Officer Crockett. When the first shot was fired thinking doubtless that a brother officer had been wounded to his death he threw himself forward between the two men. Bruce turned upon him and again his pistol blazed the bullet striking Mr. Robertson in the derangement.

JOHN W. ROBERTSON.
Special Meeting of the Board of Town Commissioners to Pay Tribute to the Memory of a Brave and Faithful Officer.
Officer.

At a special session of the Board of Commissioners of the town of Henderson, held on Saturday, April 11, 1903, the Mayor announced to the Board that on Thursday night, April 9th, 1903, Policeman John W. Robertson, while in the discharge of his duty, was fatally shot by James Bruce, colored, and died on the evening of the ensuing day. The Board took the following action:

In recognition of Mr. Robertson's worth and his services as an official of the town, and as expressing their sense of the public loss and their sympathy with his family, the following minute is unanimously adopted:

Officer Robertson has been on the police force of the town during the past two years. During that time he has been a quiet, diligent, discreet and efficient officer. The Chief of the department testifies to his uniform readiness in the performance of every duty, without regard to the hours of duty imposed upon him. He was brave. He was loyal to the public and to his fellow officers. He finally laid down his life while giving assistance to another officer.

In his death the town is deprived of the services of a good and faithful officer and this administration of one who has given it cordial and steady co-operation and support.

This Board extends to Mr. Robertson's family assurance of their warm sympathy in their sad bereavement and request that the officials of the town be permitted to testify their appreciation and respect, for the deceased by participating in the funeral service.

That the salary of Policeman Robertson be continued to his widow until the expiration of his term of office, and that all the expenses of sickness and burial be paid from the town treasury.

The Mayor is requested to appoint a committee from this Board and the officials of the town of which he shall act as chairman to make necessary arrangements for participation in the funeral exercises of Officer Robertson.

The Mayor appointed on this committee Messrs. Owen Davis and Lewis W. Barnes.

That a copy of this minute be sent to Mrs. John W. Robertson and to the GOLD LEAF with request to publish.

A true copy.

H. T. POWELL,
Town Clerk.

JUSTICE ALONE SOUGHT
Both Races Showed Commendable Discretion--- But Now Comes an Inflammatory Article by a Negro in the "True Reformer."
(Special to News and Observer.)

Henderson, N. C., April 21. There had been so much idle talk about the deplorable shooting that took place here some two weeks ago, that the mayor called a meeting of the town aldermen in order that they might look fully into the matter and see whether or not any blame should be laid at the door of Policeman Crockett. One witness, a negro boy whom Crockett thinks was the one who backed Bruce on the night of the shooting has gone, another is at Weldon and therefore there were none left to tell exactly how it all happened. So the aldermen, as best they could, weighed the statements of the generous public and the circumstances in the case and decided to exonerate Crockett so far as their blaming him as an officer. The mayor, the aldermen as a body, the policemen, and the people have been very broad in their view of the matter and at no time have they feared riot or even bodily harm to Mr. Daniels from the white people or to Policeman Crockett from the negroes.

The white people have been unusually quiet, fearing no harm and feeling no resentment toward the negro. In fact, on the day after the shooting, a white man got into a controversy with the jailer's wife and a negro man ran up and shot at the white man and the town jailed the white man because they believed he deserved it, and did nothing to the negro.

The negroes also appeared quiet and even asked the police if they might bring the body of Bruce here for burial. One of their prominent preachers gave them most excellent advice in a sermon on the 12th, after the burial of Bruce and all law-abiding citizens hoped and believed that all feeling had abated, or rather that there had been but little feeling save that of sorrow and regret. But today the people are somewhat wrought up by the article in the paper published in Littleton by a very clever negro. The paper is called the "True Reformer" and the column article on the Henderson tragedy is written and signed by M. J. Harris, a Henderson negro, and closes as follows:

"This was one of the most brutal affairs ever witnessed; two men shooting one little 20-year-old boy who weighed only about 125 pounds. The action stirred up much excitement and as one white man and one colored man are dead—the result of the brutal attack—it should give us satisfaction to know that the colored man used his gun in the protection of himself and his rights, and that he is as skillful in placing his bullets as the white man. While we lament the loss of the brave boy, Bruce, we are glad to know that he died for his rights, and gallantly sent one of his assailants on ahead of him."

INVITES TROUBLE.
Monroe J. Harris, a Henderson Negro,
Writes an Article About the Recent Tragedy Here in Which He Boldly Exults Over the Death of Policeman Robertson—"It Should Give Us Satisfaction to Know That the Colored Man Used His Gun in the Protection of Himself and His Rights, and That He is as Skillful in Placing His Bullets as the White Man," he Says—Language Calculated to Inflame Passion and Provoke Trouble.

The people of Henderson are a peaceable, law-abiding people—too conservative, perhaps—and this very spirit of conservatism seems to have been construed into a spirit of fear or cowardice by some of the negroes.

After the unfortunate occurrence week before last when two men were killed, the difficulty being brought on by the negro, it was hoped that the community would not be so stirred again. There was a great deal of feeling and considerable wild talk. All kinds of rumors were rife and excitement was high. But cool heads and calmer judgment prevailed. Further trouble was averted, if indeed there had been any danger of such, and a feeling of bitterness had given way to feelings only of regret and sorrow, when an inflammatory article, full of falsehood and misrepresentation is written by a Henderson negro and published over his signature. The article was signed by M. J. Harris and was published in the Littleton True Reformer, edited by a negro.

After relating the circumstances which led up to the trouble—the purchase of a reserved seat ticket by Bruce at Sparks' Show and seating himself among the white people; his being required to move, &e., Harris says:

"Later Mr. Bruce met and engaged in conversation with Policemen Robertson and Crockett, during which, Crockett told Bruce he was a nigger, Bruce replied that he recognized the fact that he was colored, but that he was not a nigger, but a Negro. Crockett said they were all the same, and when Bruce said they were not the same, Crockett gave him the lie and the same was returned by Bruce, at which Crockett knocked Bruce down with his billet (billy) and shot him while down, assisted by Robertson. Bruce used his gun to save himself while the two were shooting at him, and he succeeded in shooting Robertson twice, one bullet took effect in the abdomen which proved fatal. Crockett was shot once and received only a slight flesh wound as the ball struck his watch case.

"This was one of the most brutal affairs ever witnessed; two men shooting one little 20 year old boy who weighed only about 125 pounds. The action stirred up much excitement and as one white man and one colored man is dead—the result of the brutal attack—it should give us satisfaction to know that the colored man used his gun in the protection of himself and his rights, and that he is as skillful in placing his bullets as the white man.

"While we lament the loss of the brave boy Bruce, we are glad to know that he died for his rights, and gallantly sent one of his assailants on ahead of him.

"M. J. HARRIS."

Italics as above are ours.

Just as passion had subsided and it was desired that the awful tragedy should be recalled only as a memory, the inflammatory article of this insolent negro is flaunted in the faces of our people. This publication has caused great indignation and outraged public feeling. It is to be regretted that Henderson has among her citizenship, white or black, a man who would write such an article calculated to provoke trouble. Such a character is a dangerous element in any community.

A correspondent of the News and Observer, writing on the subject in Wednesday's paper, says:

"It is to be hoped that deliberate determination will take the place of idle threats and that all such, who have so strong prejudice, may be ordered to find shelter elsewhere."

A large number of the members of the United Mine Workers of America appeared before Chancellor J. C. Carmichael of the chancery court, yesterday, a rule nisi having been issued against them charging them to show cause why they should not be punished for contempt of court.

Several witnesses were examined during the day and the matter will be continued this morning at 10 o'clock.

The question at issue grows out of the original petition filed in the chancery court on August 26, by the Alabama Steel and Wire Company against Alexander Dunlap, et. als., asking that certain members of the miners' union be enjoined from trespassing on the company's property at Virginia City.

St. George, Nov. 28.—The first lynching in Dorchester county took place at Rosses, a small town about twelve miles from here, reports of which have just been received.

A NEGRO BRUTE LYNCHED.
THE USUAL CRIME HAPPENS IN DORCHESTER COUNTY.
Attempted Rape Upon a Young Lady. Wretch Trailed by Bloodhounds to His Hiding Place.
ST. GEORGE, Nov. 28.—To be chronicled in the annals of crime for Dorchester county is the deed of a rape fiend, and his summary punishment at the hands of infuriated citizens.

Another white home has been despoiled and another poor brute has been hunted with hounds and bored with buckshot.

News was received here last night of an assault by a negro upon a young lady at Ross, a station about eight miles distant from here, at 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon and immediately a posse from this place left for the scene of the trouble.

Before night there was gathered in the quiet little town of Ross a mob aggregating 200 or 300 men from the adjacent towns and country, bent upon vengeance.

Bloodhounds were put on the trail at 1:30 o'clock this morning, and before many hours passed they had hounded to his den John Fogle, a negro, the perpetrator of the heinous crime.

Speedily he was brought before his victim and identified.

The mob then, with the victim, hastened into the woods near a swamp, where the fellow had been captured, and there, to tell the dark story, is to be seen the negro's body pendant from the limb of a tree, riddled with shot.

Fortunately, by the brave fight of the lady, who is a member of a prominent family, the brute failed in his diabolical purpose, but the lady was badly bruised by being choked. It has ever been the proud boast of Dorchester county that her criminal animals contained no record of this heinous crime.

Sheriff and Deputies Brought Prisoner to Wichita.
Sheriff Patterson, Undersheriff Bartlett and County Attorney Florence arrived in Wichita yesterday morning with John Woods, the negro who criminally assaulted Mrs. John Lind, at Yates Center Tuesday evening. The prisoner was brought here after a very exciting night spent in defending him from a mob of 300 people, and then driving across the country eighteen miles to a station to catch the train.

Tuesday night the assault was made in a grove, just north of the town, and the negro was captured a few hours later in a woodshed, and locked in jail. Wednesday morning there was considerable bitter talk against the man, but during the day the excitement died down until evening.

As it began to grow dark, the eldest son of the assaulted woman began agitating the lynching of the negro and a mob was soon formed. The sheriff had received wind of the mob and collected all of his deputies and the city marshal's forces to guard the jail. A number of business men also volunteered their services. All were armed to the teeth and determined to defend the man whom they had deprived of his liberty and were duty bound to protect.

The mob went up to the jail carrying a heavy timber from the railroad yards which they intended using as a battering ram. They were met at the door by the sheriff and county attorney, who began ntalking to the crowd and begging them to let the law take its course. The mob was poorly organized and the talk of the sheriff and prominent citizens had the desired effect in that the mob disbanded and went away. They were gone but a short time when the active spirits reorganized the mob and a second attempt was made on the jail, but the guards succeeded in keeping the crowd away and finally disorganizing them for a time. The sheriff stated yesterday that he did not intend using force to drive the men away unless absolutely compelled to do so, but he was determined that they would not take the prisoner except they reached him by climbing over his body, and the men behind him were just as determined.

The men came back the third time fully determined to lynch John Wood, and again they were persuaded that it would be better for the law to take its course. The men were fewer in numbers, but more determined than ever, and things began to look dark for the sheriff and his prisoner. For three hours they had guarded the jail yard and a number of the men had spent a sleepless night Tuesday in the search for the assailant.

Close to 1 o'clock and while the mob was reorganizing for a fourth attempt a carriage was procured and the prisoner, heavily shackled, was slipped into it. Sheriff Patterson, Deputy Bartlett and the county attorney climbed in, and taking a roundabout course, got their man safely out of town, and then drove eighteen miles to Toronto, where they caught the Missouri Pacific train at 3 o'clock, which brought them to this city. They did not feel safe until they had their prisoner behind the bars of the Sedgwick county jail. All were worn out and immediately went to a hotel where they rested a few hours. The officers returned to Yates Center yesterday afternoon.

It was a most terrible experience for the officers and they do not want it to occur again. When they left here all fully believed that the excitement had died down and within a few days would die out entirely. They will leave their man here until the excitement completely subsides and he may not be taken back to Yates Center until the trial comes up in the district court, to which he was bound in the preliminary hearing Wednesday.

TWO MOBS WAIT FOR NEGRO.
When One Finishes Its Work, the Other Hangs Him.

a. Fla. Dec 5—Lewis Jackson a

Tampa, Fla., Dec. 5.—Lewis Jackson, a negro, twenty-five years old, who committed an assault on the four-year-old daughter of R. F. Ensey, of the United States Engineering Corps, at Fort Dade, at the entrance to Tampa Bay, was punished by one mob and killed by another in this city last night. There was no State law to fit Jackson's crime, and the Sheriff released him from jail last night. He was captured near the jail by a waiting mob and emasculated, the same punishment that was inflicted on a negro hackman here six months ago. He was then put in a carriage and started for the colored hospital, where physicians were in readiness to attend to his wounds.

Another mob intercepted the carriage and hanged the negro to an oak tree. The lynching was so quietly done that it was not discovered until the body was found early this morning. A coroner's jury rendered the usual verdict of death at the hands of persons unknown.
lewis-jackson-tampa-1903-12-04.A8:
THREE MOBS GOT HIM. One Beat a Negro, Another Injured Him and the Third Hanged Him.
TAMPA, Fla., Dec. 5.—Three mobs administered different degrees of punishment yesterday to Lewis Jackson, colored, aged 25, who committed an assault upon the four-year-old daughter of R. F. Ensey, an officer of the United States Engineering Corps, stationed at Fort Dade, at the entrance to Tampa Bay.

The first mob, composed of artillerymen at the fort, captured Jackson after the commission of the crime and gave him a severe beating. They were restrained with difficulty by the officers from killing him on the spot. The negro was brought to Tampa and delivered to the Sheriff, who locked him up in the county jail.

The exact offence committed by the negro being unprecedented in this State, there was no statute to cover it, and the Sheriff had to release the prisoner. Liberty was short to Jackson, however. He had gone only a short distance from the jail, when he was intercepted by a mob and taken to a small thicket near the city limits, where, by the same methods used in the case of a negro hackman, George Houston, several months ago, the victim was injured seriously.

This satisfied this mob and the negro was bundled into a cab and ordered driven to a hospital.

Jackson was released by this mob, however, only to fall into the hands of another, which stopped the cab, took him out and quickly hanged him to a limb of an oak tree. The mob dispersed, there was no shooting and the lynching was not discovered until early this morning.

Tampa, Fla., Dec. 5.—Lewis Jackson, a negro charged with having attempted to criminally assault the 3-year-old daughter of Superintendent R. F. Ensey, of the government works at Ft. DeSoto, Mullet Key, last Monday, was lynched near Tampa last night by a mob of 50 white men.

Jackson was captured soon after his crime and brought to this city where he was jailed, pending an investigation.

It was found that owing to the peculiarity of the crime, there was no law under which the negro could be convicted, and he was ordered released from jail last night.

The negro was warned that his life was in danger, and had barely reached the outskirts of the town, when he was apprehended by two white men, who placed him in a cab and carried him to a spot near the city, where a mob of white men hanged him to a tree.

PREVENT LYNCHING IN WISCONSIN.
Police Protect from Railroad Men Negro Accused by Two Little Girls.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]
on Wis. July 2.—Prompt action

Madison, Wis., July 2.—Prompt action by the police prevented the lynching of a negro within five blocks of the Capitol to-night. Ore Brown was accused by two girls, five and seven years old, of attempting to assault them. Their screams brought help, but Brown got away. He was captured later by the police, and a detail of officers was hurried to protect him from railroad men, who threatened to lynch him.

The negro was taken to the city prison, and the police prevented the gathering of any number of persons anywhere in the city to-night, especially near the jail. A conference was held with the Governor, but it was decided not to call out troops unless a mob formed.

Young Negro Arrested at Madison for Two Attempted Criminal Assaults.
MADISON, WIS.—A young negro named Ore Brown assaulted two 8-year-old white girls with criminal intent yesterday afternoon. Owing to the screams and vigorous resistance of the little girls and the approach of several who heard their cries, he failed to accomplish his purpose.

The assault occurred under a railroad bridge, half a dozen blocks from the statehouse.

Brown escaped on a bicycle, but was captured later and lodged in the police station. He is 20 years old and served a year for burglary, being released six months ago.

When the news of the assault first became known there was some talk of lynching, but the authorities do not fear any trouble.

Davis, after committing obbery early this morning. The negro got into the house wi hout disturbing the members of the Davis family and, after stealing some jewelry in the room, attacked the girl.

When the girl made an outcry the negro threatened to kill her, and then beat her on the head several times with his fists. The girl fought him, and when her screams aroused her father the negro escaped. He was caught half an hour later in a barn, to which he had been tracked by footprints in the mud. There was another negro with him, and both pretended to be asleep.

The negro attacked the girl about 3 o'clock. Four hours later the town heard of the assault and a crowd of about fifty persons gathered around the lockup. In the crowd was a number of the town hangers-on, but there were also some solid business men. One of the latter told Police Captain William H. Wilson that if the negro wasn't taken out of town before night there would be a lynching. There was no demonstration made to capture the negro, but Capt. Wilson decided that it would be wiser to have him in a stronger lockup, and he was hurried to the county jail at Freehold.

It was probably lucky for the negro that the girl, except for a few bruises where the negro struck her, was uninjured. The girl, who is pretty, is a social favorite in the town. Her father was Sheriff of Monmouth county up to a year ago and is well to do. They live in a comfortable two-story frame house on Riverside avenue.

The negro, Thomas Thomas, alias Thomas Drum, had been employed by Mayor Davis up to about a month ago, when he began to drink. It seems that although Thomas's reputation is bad, he was not feared, except when he was in his cups. Then he was known as a "bad nigger." On his record alone, however, it would appear that he was a man to be feared under any circumstances.
About twenty years ago he was a member of a gang that terrorized the town by firing houses and by robbery. He was sentenced to thirty years in prison at Trenton for that, but hadn't been there long when, with another negro named Henry Jackson, he attempted to escape. In the chase that followed Jackson and one of the keepers were killed. Thomas was recaptured, but was released on parole about two years ago for good behavior. Since then he has been doing considerable work for Mayor Davis, painting houses and doing odd jobs.

Consequently he was familiar with the Davis house and had no trouble in getting in. He first pried open the shutters on a porch window and then got inside by shoving back the latch on the window with a knife. On the porch he had removed his shoes and, in his stockings, he was able to move around the house noiselessly.

Apparently Thomas went to the pantry first and found some pork chops. These he put in a kettle and left on the porch near the door where he probably expected to get them when he made his escape from the house. His calculations were wrong, however, as the pork chops were still on the porch when he was captured.

After taking the pork chops, Thomas made his way upstairs and came to the door of Miss Davis's room, which had not been locked. Her father and the other members of the family sleep on the same floor, but at another corner of the house. It is thought that Thomas's original intention was robbery, and he went into the first room he came to, which was Miss Davis's.

A gold neckchain and bracelets belonging to Miss Davis, and a pocketbook with a five-dollar gold piece belonging to her brother, Herbert, were on a dresser. These Thomas put in his pocket, and then he went over to where the girl was sleeping.

The girl was awakened by the negro bending over her with his hands on her face. She screamed and struggled with the negro, who tried to grab her around the neck. Miss Davis, who is strong and wiry, from outdoor exercise, fought the negro, who finally whispered in her ear:

"If you don't stop screaming I will kill you."

The girl didn't stop, but went on screaming with all her lung power. The negro became furious then, and rained blow after blow on her head. Mayor Davis was awakened by his daughter's screams and came running down the hall from his room. The negro heard him coming and jumped out of the window on the roof of the porch, and from there dropped to the ground.

As he dashed down the walk to the street Mayor Davis saw the negro's outline in the dark and thought he recognized Thomas. The negro disappeared in the dark and Mr. Davis hurried around to Capt. Wilson's house a few blocks away and got the Captain out of bed. Several of the neighbors had been aroused by the girl's screams, and they joined in hunting for her assailant.

It had been raining during the night and with the aid of a lantern there was not much difficulty in following the negro's tracks in the mud. The footprints led across Riverside avenue, Front street and West street and then to a barn belonging to Mayor Davis near the railroad tracks. In a haymow in the loft of the barn Capt. Wilson found Thomas pretending to be asleep. Capt. Wilson grabbed his feet and found that the shoes were off and that the stockings were wet and muddy.

"I didn't do nothin', Loss," yelled the negro, and he jumped out of the mow and tackled Capt. Wilson. The other negro, named Daniel Webster, didn't move during the scuffle and feigned sleep. Thomas, as he fought with Capt. Wilson, kept digging into his pokcets trying to throw something out.

Finally the captain got him over his back and slipped one handcuff over his wrist. The negro punched at him with the other hand and thrust it into the other wrist band. Capt. Wilson snapped the lock and the negro was held fast. When he had Thomas secure Capt. Wilson shook the other negro and took them both to the lockup.

Meantime Mayor Davis had summoned Dr. A. G. Brown. The doctor found that Miss Davis had a cut on the back of her head and a lump over the right eye, where the negro had struck her. The girl was hysterical for a time, but soon quieted down, and it was said this afternoon that she was her natural self again.

ATTACKS HER IN ROOM.
Negro Tries to Assault Mayor's Daughter—Lynch Talk.
Red Bank, N. J., July 14.—Not since the commission of the deed for which "Mingo Jack" was lynched at Eatontown some fifteen years ago has there been so much excitement and indignation over a crime in this part of New-Jersey as was caused this morning by the acts of Thomas Thomas, alias Thomas Drum, an exconvict, who broke into the house of Mayor O. E. Davis, in Riverside-ave., and, after taking what plunder was in sight, attempted to assault Miss Grace Davis, the daughter of the Mayor, and showered blows on her when she cried for help. Thomas, too, might have been lynched had he not been hurried off to the county jail at Freehold. With Thomas, who was captured in a barn near the scene of his crime, was another negro, Daniel Webster, who was arrested as an accomplice.

The citizens were greatly aroused, and some of the most excited ones declared that Thomas ought to be burned at the stake. Chief Wilson was much relieved when the train with the negroes aboard left the station.

Red Bank, N. J., July 14.—The home of Mayor O E. Davis was burglarized early today by Thomas Thomas, alias Thomas Dunn, a negro ex-convict, who also attempted assault on Miss Grace Davis, the mayor's daughter. red-bank-red-bank-1903-08.A4:
Girl Assaulted by Burglar at Red Bank.
Burglary and assault were committed in the residence of former Sheriff Obadiah E. Davis, at Red Bank, shortly after one o'clock Tuesday morning.

The household of Mr. Davis was suddenly thrown into a state of excitement by the screaming of Miss Grace Davis who had been attacked by a burly negro who had entered her bedchamber for the purpose of theft.

Investigation disclosed the fact that the house had been burglarized. The intruder had gained an entrance by climbing to the roof of the rear piazza and entering the second story by forcing open a window. The man was not interrupted in his search through the various rooms and no one was aware of his presence until he was caught in the act of confiscating jewelry belonging to Miss Davis.

Miss Davis awakened to become aware of the fact that an intruder was in her bedchamber. Before she had time to give an alarm she received a stinging blow in the forehead. The force of the blow came near rendering her unconscious, but with great presence of mind she screamed for help. The assailant by this time had left the premises.

After assurances that there was no further danger, Miss Davis regained her composure and told her father what she knew of the affair. She suffered from a slight abrasion of the skin and was very nervous.

Sheriff Davis left his Riverside cottage in search of an officer. Chief Wilson was told of the burglary and went to the house and made an investigation.

Footprints revealed the fact that the intruder had discarded his boots. The stocking-prints were traced beyond the railroad track to a barn owned by Sheriff Davis. A search of the barn was then made. Concealed beneath the hay in the loft was a negro familiarly known as "Tom" Drum, an employee of Mr. Davis.

Drum was forced to submit to a thorough search. In his clothing was found a quantity of jewelry belonging to Miss Grace Davis.

The negro was placed under arrest and taken to the town hall. Later he was taken to Freehold to await the action of the grand jury.

After landing the prisoner safely in jail, Chief Wilson and Sheriff Davis returned to the barn and searched it thoroughly. Their efforts were rewarded by the finding of a quantity of articles that had been taken from the house, presumably by Drum. They were positively identified as property belonging to Mr. Davis.

Drum is well known in Red Bank. Several years ago when incendiary fires were frequent, Drum was arrested. He also served time in state prison for being connected with several incendiary blazes.

Since then he has been referred to as one of the fire bugs. At the expiration of his term he sought employment and was engaged by Sheriff Davis.

While in Mr. Davis' employ, Drum again got into trouble, and to save the negro from going to jail Mr. Davis went on his bond, which is still being held as security.

red-bank-red-bank-1903-08.A7:
IN PRISON A WEEK AFTER CRIME.
Negro Burglar Who Attacked Mayor's Daughter Gets Nineteen Years.
Freehold, N. J., July 20.—Thomas Thomas, colored, alias Thomas Drum, who broke into Mayor O. E. Davis's house at Red Bank a week ago to-night, is now in the State Prison at Trenton, with terms of thirty-five years before him.

The negro was tried and convicted here to-day on two indictments, one for breaking and entering the house of Mr. Davis with intent to steal and the other for assault and battery on Miss Grace Davis, his daughter, with intent to commit burglary. Miss Davis's testimony against the negro was fully corroborated. The jury was out only five minutes. Besides the nineteen year sentence, The unexpired term which Thomas will have to serve has sixteen years to run. He was sentenced to thirty years for arson and paroled after serving fourteen years. Thus, when Thomas entered prison to-day he had thirty-five years to spend there.
red-bank-red-bank-1903-08.A11:
EDITORIAL CLIPPINGS.
New Jersey has furnished two instances within the past month of the prompt administration of "Jersey justice" and of the popular preference for law over mob violence. The first case was that of the arrest, conviction and sentencing of the negro Drum at Red Bank; the other was the arrest, conviction and sentencing of a negro at Hackensack. The latter had attempted an indecent assault upon a young woman, but she was rescued and the negro was arrested. It appears that he had been raised in the South, and Judge Zabriskie, in giving him the full penalty of the law, said it was fortunate that this crime was not charged against the convict in the State from which he had come. The negro is safely in State Prison, from which he will not be released for some time, and Hackensack, like Red Bank, has no foul blot upon her fair name.—Newark News.
red-bank-red-bank-1903-08.A13:
It Certainly Makes a Difference.
On one page of the New York Sun of Wednesday last we find two columns of report of three outrageous assaults by negroes, one near Red Bank, New Jersey, one near Trenton, New Jersey, and the third near Albany, New York. In two of the cases lynching was narrowly averted. The day before the same paper was full of the story of a riot in the streets of New York, negroes and whites being in conflict. Possibly, now that the subject is coming close to the homes of these northern people, they will begin to discover its difficulties. When at a distance it seems easy of solution. Close at hand it is not so.—Mobile Register.

Advertiser Bureau. Mobile, May 25.

In the City Council room promptly at the noon hour, order was called, the Inferior Criminal Court having moved there in order to hold the preliminary trial of Marion L. Daugherty, Jack Strong and H. Ross Rogers, white charged with the killing of Richard Smith, a negro, at or near the Mobile Lumber Company's mill on the Louisville and Nashville Railroad, about a half mile north of One-Mile Creek, on Saturday, mention of which appeared in yesterday's Advertiser.

Judge Jules E. Alford presided and the state was represented by Solicitor Webb. Several attorneys were present for the defense. Three whites and twenty negroes were present as witnesses, besides a number of character witnesses.

Prior to the preliminary examination the coroner held an inquest and recommended the holding of Rogers.

A number of character witnesses, by agreement, were first examined, because of these being in business. Among these were President J. W. Whiting of the People's Bank, Lloyd Batre, insurance man; Robert Neville, merchant; Mr. Rosengrant, lumber business; N. R. Clarke, attorney.

For the State, the solicitor stated that, by agreement, the coroner, Dr. Hirshfield, would testify as to the location of the wounds, of which there were three. Attorney for defendants offered an interjection as to the position of the wounded man (deceased) at the time of the cutting. The solicitor held the Supreme Court had already ruled on this point, and that, even if the physician did testify, it would not be competent. No ruling.

Dan Morisette was the first witness. He said he was present at the office at the time of the killing. Smith told Mr. Daugherty his time was wrong. Daugherty asked Rogers to look it up. He said the time was right. Smith said something about the law and was ordered out. Did not see the outside affair. Told of the location of the office and window. Smith was at the window.

Dr. W. T. Henderson (admitted to be an expert)—When I saw the man he was dead. Had slight wound on shoulder, deep cut on leg which severed femoral artery. Clothing was cut in several places around shoulder and back and on leg of pants near thigh.

John Reed—I and Richard Smith were at window. There was words about the money. When ordered away Smith said he would see it cost them more. As he walked away Rogers jumped off the gallery and struck Smith, who struck back. When Rogers came out Daugherty jumped up and said let's kill the . Rogers struck first blow. As Smith was going away Daugherty struck at him with a stick. Smith got to the railroad and Rogers overtook him. Smith struck Rogers and they clinched. Smith had Rogers's head under his arm and Rogers began, as I thought, striking him. I said, "That white man is giving that nigger the devil." Mr. Daugherty ran up and shot and the pistol flew up. Rogers and Smith did not get down on the ground. Did not see Smith pick up anything as he ran up the bank. Did not see where Daugherty got the pistol. He followed Smith about ten yards. Had the pistol pointed at Smith's head. When it fired it was up.

Witness identified hat of deceased. It had a burned spot on the brim when he last saw it, but no hole. (Hat had hole in it when presented in court.)

Cross—Daugherty was in his office when he said "Let's kill the black ." Rogers was going out then. There were two or three others around the window, the crowd had gone away from the window. Some one was practicing shooting, but I didn't know who they were. When Daugherty first had the pistol, if he had fired it would have gone through Smith's head.

Alex Reed—Was where the men were shooting at target. Strong had the gun and Mr. Daugherty said behind us: "Let me get my gun and kill the——." Mr. Strong said here's one. Daugherty took it and started towards Rogers and Smith. He shot and turned back and when I said to him "I didn't think you would shoot a man that way," he said, "I didn't shoot him, I shot to scare him. He wasn't shot, he was cut." When Daugherty cursed he threw a stick at Smith. When I next saw Daugherty he had a gun. It appeared to me the pistol was ranging on the man. Don't see how it kept from hitting Smith.

Cross—Daugherty was close enough to hit Smith with the pistol two minutes. He was about three feet away. Did not see a knife. Saw blood at the scuffle and also where the man fell.

THREE MEN WOUNDED IN MARYLAND RIOT
Whites and Negroes Battle at Hurlock Over a Game of Craps.
CAMBRIDGE, Md., Nov. 4.—Hurlock, a thriving town of 500 inhabitants at the junction of the Baltimore, Chesapeake, and Atlantic and Cambridge and Seaford Roads, was the scene last night of a race war, in which three whites and one negro were wounded.

The trouble began Saturday night over a game of craps between some white and negro'boys. It is said that the negroes won all the money and the whites resented it by trying to "clean them up." Last night at 11 o'clock the negroes began firing at the whites and the fire was returned.

Sheriff John W. Mills, Deputy Gore, and Richard Hughlett were sent to the scene from Cambridge and Deputy W. J. Watkins, and a posse from East New Market. Fourteen negroes were arrested and lodged in the Cambridge jail this morning.
samuel-parvin-young-hurlock-1903-11-03.A4:
WARFIELD THE WINNER
Returns Indicate Victory For the Democrats in Maryland.
Baltimore, Md., Nov. 3.—At 1 o'clock this morning the returns from Baltimore and the Maryland counties are meagre owing to the length of the ballot and therefore it is impossible to give the result.

The indications, however, point to the election of Edwin Warfield, (Dem.), as Governor, over Stenson A. Williams, (Rep.), and that the Legislature, which will elect a United States senator, will also be Democratic.

Baltimore, Nov. 4.—At 2 a. m. only eighty-five of the 308 voting precincts of Baltimore city had been reported to the election supervision officers. If this ratio of Democratic gains are continued Warfield (Dem.) has carried the city by 7,000 to 8,000 plurality.

Returns from the counties are meagre, but it is not thought that the Republicans in the State can overcome the Democratic plurality in Baltimore city.

As far as known here at this hour the election of Tuesday passed off peaceably throughout the State except in one instance. In Hurlock, Dorchester County, there is said to have been a dispute between whites and blacks in which it is reported twelve men were wounded. Owing to congested telegraph service tonight the report cannot be verified.
samuel-parvin-young-hurlock-1903-11-03.A5:
RACE CLASH IN MARYLAND.
Fourteen Negroes in Jail in Cambridge Four White Men Wounded.
CAMBRIDGE, Md., Nov. 4.—A race fight occurred at Hurlock last night, and as a result fourteen negroes are in Cambridge jail. Trouble between the races at Hurlock had been brewing for some time. On Tuesday afternoon the negroes collected from their homes around Hurlock and entered the town, saying that they intended to take the place. They began firing upon the white people at night and a fight ensued.

The negroes put out the street lights, shot the lights out of windows and poured shots upon the white people. Four young men were wounded, but their injuries are not serious.

The citizens of the town telephoned to Cambridge to Sheriff Mills for assistance. Sheriff Mills, Deputy Sheriff Gora, W. J. Watkins and Richard Hughlett left immediately for Hurlock and were joined on the way by a posse from East Newmarket.

They arrested and brought to Cambridge fourteen negroes, some of whom are said to be tough characters. Other arrests will likely follow. Reports from Hurlock this morning say the disturbance is not yet entirely quieted. The four young men shot were Samuel Parvin Young, Mr. Bennett, son of James Bennett, a Mr. Medford and Mr. MacFarland, a son of the Rev. MacFarland, pastor of the Methodist Episcopal Church at Williamsburg. Several of the negroes in the Cambridge jail have shots in their bodies.

Trouble Grew Out of Killing of Negro Farmer.

Thomasville, Ga., Aug. 31.—The people in the vicinity of Ocklocknee, a Thomas county town twelve miles north of Thomasville, are in a ferment of excitement over a threatened race war with the negroes of that neighborhood. The trouble was started by the mysterious killing on Friday night of Thomas Williams, a negro farmer who lived four miles northeast of Ocklocknee. He was called out of his house about 9 o'clock at night by unknown parties. A few moments afterwards shots were heard and he was found in a dying condition a short distance from his house by his wife.

The verdict of the coroner's jury was that Williams came to his death by the hands of parties unknown. Williams' wife, however, accuses a well known young white man of Ocklocknee of the crime. He, however, is able to prove a complete alibi.

A large number of negroes attended Williams' funeral and seemed excited and discontented. Several were heard to make complaints, and one made the statement that the trouble had not yet started. On Saturday night Williams' brother bought 159 cartridges in an Ocklocknee hardware store, and pistols, cartridges and firearms were freely purchased by other negroes. These suspicious actions put the white people on their guard. Every family in the neighborhood was warned, and they are all ready for trouble if it should arise.

The white people are in a majority in this district, and any conflict that should arise could have but one result. The negroes are kept under a close watch, especially those of the turpentine stills, who are of a turbulent class.

The white people are among the most conservative in the county, and they give assurance that they will take no radical measures, and will act only on the defensive. Cooler heads among the negroes realize this also, and it is practically certain that trouble will be averted. Sunday passed quietly with no new developments in the affair.
